title: Foot shape changes: when a deformity needs care
intro: Feet vary naturally in arch height, toe alignment and flexibility. Flat arches, high arches, bunions and curled toes are different findings, not one diagnosis. Appearance alone does not establish disease or the need for correction. Pain, walking, skin pressure and whether a change is new guide assessment.

sections.heading: Describe symptoms and progression
paragraphs: Note where pain occurs, which shoes aggravate it and whether the foot changes shape when standing. Mention injuries, weakness, numbness, diabetes or arthritis. A clinician checks skin, circulation, sensation, joints and walking. Imaging may help selected cases but is not automatically required for every unusual-looking foot.

sections.heading: Distinguish flexible variation from a new problem
paragraphs: Painless flexible flat feet in children often need reassurance rather than corrective products. A stiff, painful, one-sided or newly changing foot needs assessment. High arches with weakness or sensory change can justify neurological investigation. Avoid diagnosing from a footprint or assuming that all flat feet cause back or knee pain.

sections.heading: Make footwear and pressure relief practical
paragraphs: Choose adequate width and toe space, a secure fit and a sole suited to your activity. Check rubbing and skin, especially with reduced sensation. Pads or insoles may relieve symptoms but do not reliably reshape every deformity. Have aids fitted and reviewed; stop using a device causing sores and seek advice rather than wearing through pain.

sections.heading: Match treatment to function and goals
paragraphs: Exercises, activity adaptation, physiotherapy or podiatry may help particular problems. Surgery is considered when significant symptoms persist and the expected benefit outweighs risks, not simply to achieve an ideal appearance. Ask about recovery, weight-bearing restrictions, recurrence and possible stiffness. Avoid forceful correction or cutting corns yourself, particularly with diabetes or circulation problems.

sections.heading: Recognize urgent changes and review progress
paragraphs: A hot swollen foot, an infected wound, rapidly worsening deformity, inability to bear weight after injury or a cold pale foot needs prompt assessment. With diabetes or reduced sensation, serious damage may cause little pain. Seek review for persistent discomfort or new loss of function. Agree a measurable goal, such as walking comfortably in suitable shoes, and revisit treatment if it does not help.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: painless childhood arches
examples.text: Mira’s child has flat flexible feet but plays comfortably. The family asks about development rather than buying expensive corrective shoes solely because of appearance.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: checking pressure
examples.text: Arben notices a sore spot beneath an insole and has reduced foot sensation. He stops using the offending aid and seeks assessment instead of assuming discomfort proves the device is working.
